SIAA (1906) | awards = | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 1954 | CFBHOF_id = 1297 }} '''John William Heisman''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|h|aɪ|z|m|ə|n}} {{respell|HYZE|mən}}; October 23, 1869 – October 3, 1936) was an American sportsman, writer, and actor. He was a player and coach of [[American football]], [[baseball]], and [[basketball]], and served as the head football coach at [[Oberlin College]], Buchtel College (now known as the [[University of Akron]]), [[Auburn University]], [[Clemson University]], [[Georgia Tech]], the [[University of Pennsylvania]], [[Washington & Jefferson Presidents football|Washington & Jefferson College]], and [[Rice University]], compiling a career [[college football]] coaching record of 186–70–18. Heisman was also the head basketball coach at Georgia Tech, tallying a mark of 9–14, and the head baseball coach at Buchtel, Clemson, and Georgia Tech, amassing a career [[college baseball]] record of 199–108–7. He served as the [[athletic director]] at Georgia Tech and Rice. While at Georgia Tech, he was also the president of the [[Atlanta Crackers]] baseball team. Sportswriter [[Fuzzy Woodruff]] dubbed Heisman the "pioneer of [[Southern United States|Southern]] football".{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928b|page=32}} He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] as a coach in 1954. His entry there notes that Heisman "stands only behind [[Amos Alonzo Stagg]], [[Pop Warner]], and [[Walter Camp]] as a master innovator of the brand of football of his day". He was instrumental in several changes to the game, including legalizing the [[forward pass]]. The [[Heisman Trophy]], awarded annually to the season's most outstanding college football player, is named after him. ==Early life and playing career== {{stack|float=left|[[File:HeismanPose.jpg|left|thumb|upright=0.6|Heisman as a player while a student at [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]], 1891]]}} John Heisman was born Johann Wilhelm Heisman{{refn|group=n|The name John William was later adopted to obscure the fact that he was the son of immigrants. His father was ostensibly the estranged son of German aristocrats.{{cite web|url=http://pabook2.libraries.psu.edu/palitmap/bios/Heisman__John.html|title=Heisman, John William|website=libraries.psu.edu|access-date=October 6, 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122024724/http://pabook2.libraries.psu.edu/palitmap/bios/Heisman__John.html|archive-date=January 22, 2016}}{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|pages=3–6}} His mother's grandfather had been an ''aide-de-campe'' to [[Napoleon]].{{cite web|url=http://technique.library.gatech.edu/issues/fall1997/oct10/campuslife3.html|title=Heisman led Jackets to victory|author=Pat Edwards|access-date=January 9, 2017|website=technique.library.gatech.edu}}}} on October 23, 1869, in [[Cleveland|Cleveland, Ohio]], the son of [[Bavaria]]n [[German people|German]] immigrant Johann Michael Heissmann and Sara Lehr Heissmann. He grew up in northwestern Pennsylvania near [[Titusville, Pennsylvania|Titusville]] and was [[salutatorian]] of his graduating class at [[Titusville Area High School|Titusville High School]].{{Harvnb|Brandt|2001|pages=53–54}} His oration at his graduation entitled "The Dramatist as Sermonizer" was described as "full of dramatic emphasis and fire, and showed how the masterpieces of [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare]] depicted the ends of unchecked passion."{{Cite news |last=Weber |first=David L. |date=June 13, 2015 |title=The John Heisman Story: 'Father of the forward pass,' Titusville's most noted sports figure. |url=http://www.titusvilleherald.com/sports/article_fab04f06-1184-11e5-a4e2-ef3c2f62e574.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101100757/https://www.titusvilleherald.com/sports/article_fab04f06-1184-11e5-a4e2-ef3c2f62e574.html |archive-date=November 1, 2020 |access-date=January 18, 2017 |work=Titusville Herald}} Although he was a drama student, he confessed he was "football mad". He played [[Varsity team#Varsity in North America|varsity]] football for Titusville High School from 1884 to 1886. Heisman's father refused to watch him play at Titusville, calling football "bestial".{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=120}} Heisman went on to play football as a [[Lineman (gridiron football)|lineman]] at [[Brown University]] and at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/5157614/the_atlanta_constitution/|work=The Atlanta Constitution|title=Football Master Strategist New Name For Heisman|date=October 13, 1918|page=3|access-date=May 4, 2016|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/1924578/the_atlanta_constitution/|title=Heisman's Playing Record|work=The Atlanta Constitution |date=November 29, 1903|page=11|access-date=October 8, 2016|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}} He also played baseball at Penn.{{Harvnb|Buchtel College Alumni Association|1922|page=244}} On [[Brown Bears football|Brown's football team]], he was a substitute [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] in 1887, and a starting [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|tackle]] in 1888. At [[Penn Quakers football|Penn]], he was a substitute [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] in 1889, a substitute center and tackle in [[1890 Penn Quakers football team|1890]], and a starting [[End (gridiron football)|end]] in [[1891 Penn Quakers football team|1891]]. Sportswriter [[Edwin Pope]] tells us Heisman was "a 158-pound center ... in constant dread that his immediate teammates{{mdash}}guards weighing 212 and 243{{mdash}}would fall on him."{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=119}} He had a flat nose due to being struck in the face by a [[Ball (gridiron football)|football]], when he tried to block a kick against [[1890 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]] by [[Leapfrog|leap-frogging]] the center. Heisman graduated from the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]] in 1892.{{cite web |url=http://www.archives.upenn.edu/people/1800s/heisman_john.html |title=John Heisman (1869–1936) |work=Penn Biographies |publisher=Penn University Archives & Records Center|access-date=December 24, 2013}} Due to poor eyesight, he took his exams orally.{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/3626273/heisman-trophy/|title=How the Heisman Trophy Got Its Name|author=Lily Rothman|date=December 12, 2014|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|access-date=January 2, 2018}}{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=42}} ==Coaching career== In his book ''Principles of Football'', Heisman described his coaching strategy: "The coach should be masterful and commanding, even dictatorial. He has no time to say 'please' or 'mister'. At times he must be severe, arbitrary, and little short of a [[czar]]."{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=126}}{{Harvnb|Heisman|1922|page=360}} Heisman always used a [[megaphone]] at practice.{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=127}} "Heisman's voice was deep, his diction perfect, his tone biting." He was also known for his use of [[Syllable|polysyllabic]] language, and would repeat this annually, at the start of each football season:{{cite web |url=http://www.petroleumhistory.org/OilHistory/pages/Heisman/john_heisman.html |title=John Heisman, Football Coach |website=Oil History |last=Pees |first=Samuel T. |access-date=November 12, 2014}} {{quote|What is this? It is a [[prolate spheroid]], an elongated sphere in which the outer [[leather]] casing is drawn tightly over a somewhat smaller [[rubber]] tubing. Better to have died as a small boy than to [[fumble]] this football.}} ===Early coaching career: Oberlin and Buchtel=== Heisman first coached at Oberlin College. In 1892, ''The Oberlin Review'' wrote: "Mr. Heisman has entirely remade our football. He has taught us scientific football."{{cite web|url=https://www.postandcourier.com/sports/john-heisman-the-man-behind-the-award-and-his-time-at-clemson/article_fbd743ed-05de-5ac1-9184-c6aa40c52b9b.html|title=John Heisman: The man behind the award and his time at Clemson|first=Travis|last=Sawchik|date=December 7, 2012|website=postandcourier.com|access-date=December 24, 2017}} He used the [[double pass]], from tackle to [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]],{{cite journal|author=J. W. Heisman|date=October 1908|title=Inventions In Football|url=http://www.archives.upenn.edu/histy/features/sports/football/heisman_article.pdf|journal=The Baseball Magazine|volume=1|pages=40–42|number=6}} and moved his [[quarterback]] to the [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] position on [[American football#Defensive unit|defense]].{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=228}} Influenced by [[1891 Yale Bulldogs football team|Yale]] and [[Pudge Heffelfinger]], Heisman implemented the now illegal "[[flying wedge#Sports|flying wedge]]" [[Formation (American football)|formation]].{{cite web|url=https://newrepublic.com/article/74483/colle-football-bans-wedge-blocking-kickoffs|title=College Football Bans Wedge Blocking On Kickoffs|author=Jonathan Chait|date=April 16, 2010|website=newrepublic.com|access-date=January 1, 2018}} It involved seven players arranged as a "V" to protect the ball carrier.{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=121}} Heisman was also likely influenced by Heffelfinger to [[Pulling (American football)|pull]] guards on [[end run]]s.{{Harvnb|Umphlett|1992|page=32}}{{Harvnb|Brandt|2001|page=71}} [[File:Oberlin College football team, 1892.jpg|thumb|The 1892 Oberlin football team: Heisman on the left in the middle row.]] On his [[1892 Oberlin Yeomen football team|1892 team]], Heisman's [[Athletic trainer|trainer]] was Clarence Hemingway, the father of author [[Ernest Hemingway]] and one of his linemen was the first [[Native Hawaiian|Hawaiian]] to play college football, the future politician [[John Henry Wise]].{{cite journal|last1=Williams|first1=Ronald Jr. |year=2012|title=To Raise a Voice in Praise: The Revivalist Mission of John Henry Wise, 1889–1896|url=https://evols.library.manoa.hawaii.edu/bitstream/10524/33792/1/HJH46_1-36.pdf.pdf|journal=Hawaiian Journal of History|publisher=Hawaiian Historical Society|volume=46|pages=1–35|hdl=10524/33792}}{{cite web|url=http://www.midweek.com/first-native-football-player/|title=The First Native Football Player|author=Bob Hogue|date=March 5, 2015|website=midweek.com|access-date=December 24, 2017}} The team beat [[1892 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]] twice and considered itself undefeated at the end of the season. However, the outcome of its game against [[1892 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]] is still in dispute. Michigan declared it had won the game, 26–24, but Oberlin said it won 24–22. The [[Official (American football)#Referee|referee]], an Oberlin substitute player, had ruled that time had expired. The [[Official (American football)#Umpire|umpire]], a Michigan supporter, ruled otherwise. Michigan's [[George Jewett]], who had scored all of his team's points and was the school's first [[African Americans|black]] player, then ran for a [[touchdown]] with no Oberlin players on the [[American football field|field]]. ''The Michigan Daily'' and ''Detroit Tribune'' reported that Michigan had won the game, while ''The Oberlin News'' and ''The Oberlin Review'' reported that Oberlin had won.{{cite web|title=The Day Oberlin Beat Michigan, Or Did We? |author=Geoffrey Blodgett |publisher=Oberlin Alumni Magazine |date=Winter 1999 |url=http://www.oberlin.edu/alummag/oamcurrent/oam_winter99/atissue.html |access-date=March 7, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229214420/http://www.oberlin.edu/alummag/oamcurrent/oam_winter99/atissue.html |archive-date=February 29, 2012|url-status=live }} In 1893, Heisman became the football and baseball coach at Buchtel College. A disappointing baseball season was made up for by a 5–2 [[1893 Buchtel football team|football season]].{{Harvnb|Buchtel College Alumni Association|1922|page=245}} It was then customary for the center to begin a [[American football plays|play]] by rolling or kicking the ball backwards, but this proved difficult for Buchtel's unusually tall quarterback Harry Clark.{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|pages=64–65}}{{refn|group=n|Former Yale center [[Pa Corbin]] described how one used to snap the ball with his foot: "By standing the ball on end and exercising a certain pressure on the same, it was possible to have it bound into the quarterback's hands."{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-WktAQAAMAAJ&q=%22field+frequently%22|journal=Harper's Weekly|date=November 29, 1913|page=26|title=Current Athletics|first=Herbert |last=Reed|volume=58}}}} Under Heisman, the center began tossing the ball to Clark, a practice that eventually evolved into the [[Snap (gridiron football)|snap]].{{Harvnb|Umphlett|1992|page=37}} The first school to officially defeat Heisman was [[1893 Case football team|Case School of Applied Science]], known today as [[Case Western Reserve Spartans football|Case Western Reserve]].{{cn|date=October 2025}} Buchtel won [[1894 Buchtel football team|a single game]] against [[1894 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]] at the [[Ohio State Fair]]{{Harvnb|Buchtel College Alumni Association|1922|page=246}} before Heisman returned to Oberlin in [[1894 Oberlin Yeomen football team|1894]], posting a 4–3–1 record, including losses to [[1894 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]] and undefeated [[1894 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]].{{Harvnb|Oberlin College|2008|page=34}} The Penn State game ended with a [[fair catch]] and [[Fair catch kick|free kick]], which resulted in a [[field goal]] for Penn State. Referees were confused whether teams could kick a field goal or had to [[Punt (gridiron football)|punt]] on a free kick, and the game ended 6–4 in favor of Oberlin, but Walter Camp over-ruled the game officials, allowing Penn State its extra free kick and the victory 9–6.{{Harvnb|Brandt|2001|page=144}} ===Auburn=== [[File:HeismanatAuburn.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.6|Heisman at Auburn|alt=Portrait of Heisman in his mid- to late twenties at Auburn University]] After his two years at Oberlin and possibly due to the economic [[Panic of 1893]], Heisman invested his savings and began working at a tomato farm in [[Marshall, Texas]].{{Cite journal|last=Draughon|first=Ralph Jr.|date=Spring 2013|title=Coach John Heisman on Stage at Auburn|journal=Alabama Heritage|pages=28–33}} It was hard work in the heat and Heisman was losing money.{{Harvnb|Clemson University|2016b|page=168}}{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=77}} He was contacted by [[Walter Riggs]], then the manager of the Alabama Polytechnic Institute ([[Auburn University]]) [[Auburn Tigers football|football team]]. Auburn was looking for a football coach, and Heisman was suggested to Riggs by his former player at Oberlin, [[1895 Penn Quakers football team|Penn]]'s then-captain [[Carl S. Williams]]. For a salary of $500, he accepted a part-time job as a "trainer". Heisman coached football at Auburn from [[1895 Auburn Tigers football team|1895]] to [[1899 Auburn Tigers football team|1899]]. Auburn's yearbook, the ''Glomerata'', in 1897 stated "Heisman came to us in the fall of '95, and the day on which he arrived at Auburn can well be marked as the luckiest in the history of athletics at the Alabama Polytechnic Institute." At Auburn, Heisman had the idea for his quarterback to call out "hike" or "hep" to start a play and receive the ball from the center, or to draw the opposing team into an [[Offside (American football)|offside]] [[Penalty (gridiron football)|penalty]]. He also used a fake snap to draw the other team offsides.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/6939703/the_atlanta_constitution/|title=New Football Rules Concise, Complete|last=Heisman|first=J. W.|date=September 4, 1904|work=The Atlanta Constitution|access-date=October 8, 2016|page=3|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}} He began his use of a type of delayed buck play where an end took a [[hand-off]], then handed the ball to the halfback on the opposite side, who [[Rush (gridiron football)|rushed]] up the middle.{{Harvnb|Umphlett|1992|page=53}} As a coach, Heisman "railed and snorted in practice, imploring players to do their all for God, country, Auburn, and Heisman. Before each game he made squadmen take a nonshirk, nonflinch oath."{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=122}} Due to his fondness for Shakespeare, he would sometimes use a British accent at practice.{{Harvnb|Schafer|2004|page=11}} While it was then illegal to coach from the sidelines during a game, Heisman would sometimes use secret signals with a bottle or a handkerchief to communicate with his team. [[File:1895 Auburn - Georgia football game at Piedmont Park in Atlanta Georgia.jpg|thumb|Auburn vs. Georgia in 1895]] Heisman's first game as an Auburn coach came against [[1895 Vanderbilt Commodores football team|Vanderbilt]]. Heisman had his quarterback [[Reynolds Tichenor]] use the "[[hidden ball trick]]" to tie the game at 6 points.{{Harvnb|Schafer|2004|page=12}}{{Harvnb|Woodbery|2012|page=102}} However, Vanderbilt answered by kicking a field goal and won 9–6, making it the first game of Southern football decided by a field goal.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=897&dat=19310124&id=-aNaAAAAIBAJ&pg=4042,1045626|title=Sport Slants|last=Gould|first=Alan|date=January 24, 1931|work=Prescott Evening Courier}} In the [[Deep South's Oldest Rivalry|rivalry]] game with [[1895 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]], Auburn won 16–6. Georgia coach Pop Warner copied the hidden ball trick, and in 1903, his [[1903 Carlisle Indians football team|Carlisle]] team famously used it to defeat [[1903 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]].{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=41}}{{cite news|url=https://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19311019-01.2.46&e=-------en-20--21--txt-txIN-student+army+training+corps------#|title=How Pop Fooled Harvard|author=Feg Murray|date=October 19, 1931|work=The Stanford Daily|volume=80|issue=13}} Earlier in the [[1895 college football season|1895 season]], Heisman witnessed [[1895 Georgia vs. North Carolina football game|one of the first illegal forward passes]] when [[1895 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]] faced [[1895 North Carolina Tar Heels football team|North Carolina]] in [[Atlanta]]. Georgia was about to block a punt when UNC's [[Joel Whitaker]] tossed the ball out of desperation, and [[George Stephens (American football)|George Stephens]] caught the pass and ran 70 yards for a touchdown.{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=116}} Georgia coach Pop Warner complained to the referee that the play was illegal, but the referee let the play stand because he did not see the pass.{{cite web | url=http://www.tarheeltimes.com/2006/08/tar_heels_credi.html | title=Tar Heels Credited with Throwing First Forward Pass | access-date=July 12, 2011| work=Tar Heel Times| publisher=tarheeltimes.com |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061219050634/http://www.tarheeltimes.com/2006/08/tar_heels_credi.html |archive-date = December 19, 2006}} Later, Heisman became one of the main proponents of making the forward pass legal. [[File:1896 Auburn football team.jpg|thumb|1896 Auburn team, Heisman standing on the right]] Lineman [[Marvin Pearce|Marvin "Babe" Pearce]] had transferred to Auburn from [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama]], and Reynolds Tichenor was captain of the [[1896 Auburn Tigers football team|1896 Auburn team]], which beat [[1896 Georgia Tech football team|Georgia Tech]] 45–0.{{cite web|url=http://www.tuscaloosanews.com/news/20081128/believe-it-or-not-player--was-a-tider-then-a-tiger|title=Believe it or not: Player was a Tider, then a Tiger|last=Palmer|first=Michael E.|date=November 28, 2008}} Auburn players greased the train tracks the night before the game. Georgia Tech's train did not stop until [[Loachapoka]], and the Georgia Tech players had to walk the 5 miles back to Auburn.{{cite web|url=https://www.si.com/vault/1993/12/17/8221714/heisman-to-shug-from-the-arrival-of-john-heisman-in-1895-to-the-departure-of-shug-jordan-in-1975-auburn-nurtured-a-rich-football-tradition|title=HEISMAN TO SHUG From the arrival of John Heisman in 1895 to the departure of Shug Jordan in 1975, Auburn nurtured a rich football tradition|author=Ed Hinton|website=si.com|date=December 17, 1993}} This began a tradition of students parading through the streets in their pajamas, known as the "[[Auburn University traditions#Wreck Tech Pajama Parade|Wreck Tech Pajama Parade]]".{{cite web|url=http://www.ocm.auburn.edu/news_releases/wrecktech05.html|title=WRECK TECH PAJAMA PARADE, PEP RALLY SET FOR FRIDAY EVENING|date=August 30, 2005|author=David M. Granger|website=www.ocm.auburn.edu}} Auburn finished the season by losing 12–6 to Pop Warner's [[Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association]] champion [[1896 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]] team, which was led by quarterback [[Richard Von Albade Gammon]].{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=68}} Auburn received its first national publicity when Heisman was able to convince ''[[Harper's Weekly]]'' to publish the 1896 team's photo. The [[1897 Auburn Tigers football team|1897 Auburn team]] featured linemen Pearce and [[John Penton (American football)|John Penton]], a transfer from [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Virginia]]. Of its three games, one was a scoreless tie against [[1897 Sewanee Tigers football team|Sewanee]], "[[Sewanee: The University of the South|The University of the South]]" in Tennessee.{{Harvnb|Auburn University|2009|page=182}} Another was a 14–4 defeat of [[Nashville Garnet and Blue football|Nashville]], which featured [[Bradley Walker]].{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/20178869/the_tennessean/|title=Dixie's Football Hall of Fame|author=J. W. Heisman|page=35|date=February 7, 1915|work=The Tennessean|access-date=May 24, 2018|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}} Tichenor had transferred to [[1897 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]]. Gammon moved to [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] and died in the game against [[1897 Virginia Cavaliers football team|Virginia]].{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=71}} Auburn finished the 1897 football season $700 in debt, and in response, Heisman took on the role of a theater producer and staged the [[Comedy|comedic]] [[Play (theatre)|play]] ''[[David Garrick (play)|David Garrick]]''.{{cite news|url=https://issuu.com/theplainsman/docs/06.06.13_edition_of_the_auburn_plai|title=John Heisman, from sidelines to center stage|work=The Auburn Plainsman|date=June 6, 2013|author=Jeffrey Moore}} Having made enough money for another football season, the [[1898 Auburn Tigers football team|1898 team]] won two out of three games, with its loss coming against undefeated [[1898 North Carolina Tar Heels football team|North Carolina]]. After falling behind 13–4 to [[1898 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]], Heisman started using fullback George Mitcham, and won the game 18–17.{{Harvnb|Umphlett|1992|page=55}} The 1899 team, which Heisman considered his best while at Auburn,{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/1944523//|work=Atlanta Constitution|title=Brown Calls Vanderbilt '06 Best Eleven South Ever Had|date=February 19, 1911|access-date=March 8, 2015|page=52|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}} was led by fullback [[Arthur Feagin]]. As Heisman recalled, "I do not think I have ever seen so fast a team as that was."{{Cite web |last=Henderson |first=Jeremy |date=August 18, 2013 |title=John Heisman: Auburn 'the first to show what could be done' with the hurry-up offense |url=https://www.thewareaglereader.com/2013/08/john-heisman-on-auburns-hurry-up-offense/#.VFE0TefOSDo |access-date=June 28, 2025 |website=The War Eagle Reader}} Auburn was leading [[1899 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]] by a score of 11–6 when the game was called due to darkness, lighting not being available at that time, resulting in an official scoreless tie.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/16520431/the_atlanta_constitution/|title=With Auburn 11 Points To Georgia's 6, Referee Ends The Fast Contest And Result Is A Draw|date=November 19, 1899|work=The Atlanta Constitution|access-date=January 14, 2018|page=5|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}} Heisman fitted his linemen with straps and handles under their belts so that the other linemen could hold onto them and prevent the opposing team from breaking through the line. The umpire W. L. Taylor had to cut them. Most notable perhaps is the [[1922 Alabama vs. Penn football game|9–7 loss]] to [[1922 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama]] in 1922, the Crimson Tide's first major intersectional victory.{{Harvnb|Kordic|2007|page=9}} In 1923, Heisman coached the [[Washington & Jefferson Presidents football|Washington and Jefferson Presidents]], which beat the previously undefeated [[1923 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|West Virginia Mountaineers]].{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/west-virginia/1923-schedule.html |website=sports-reference.com |title=1923 West Virginia Mountaineers Schedule and Results |access-date=January 9, 2017 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160924213211/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/west-virginia/1923-schedule.html |archive-date=September 24, 2016 }} ===Rice=== Following the season at Washington and Jefferson College, Heisman ended his coaching career with four seasons at [[Rice University|Rice]]. W. Heisman New Coach|date=February 19, 1924}} His teams saw little success, and he earned more than any faculty member.{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=198}} Rice was his last coaching job before he retired in 1927 to lead the [[Downtown Athletic Club]] in [[Manhattan]], New York.{{Harvnb|Pennington|2009|page=10}} In 1935, the Downtown Athletic Club began awarding a Downtown Athletic Club trophy for the best football player east of the [[Mississippi River]]. ==Personal life== Heisman met his first wife, an actress, while he was participating in theater during his time at Clemson.{{Cite web|url=http://www.encyclopedia.com/people/sports-and-games/sports-biographies/john-william-heisman|title=John William Heisman facts, information, pictures {{!}} Encyclopedia.com articles about John William Heisman|website=www.encyclopedia.com|language=en|access-date=January 18, 2017}} Evelyn McCollum Cox, whose stage name was Evelyn Barksdale, was a widow with a single child, a 12-year-old boy named Carlisle.{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=111}} They married during the 1903 season, on October 24, 1903, a day after Heisman's 34th birthday. While in Atlanta, Heisman also shared the house with the family [[poodle]] named Woo. He would feed the dog ice cream.{{cite journal|url=https://issuu.com/gtalumni/docs/vol90_no1_low_res/19|title=Tech Pet Hall of Fame|volume=90|number=1|year=2014|journal=Georgia Tech Alumni Magazine|page=19}} In 1918, Heisman and his wife divorced, and to prevent any social embarrassment to his former wife, who chose to remain in the city, he left Atlanta after the 1919 football season. Carlisle and Heisman would remain close. Heisman met Edith Maora Cole, a student at Buchtel College, where he was coaching football during the 1893 and 1894 seasons. The two were close, but decided not to marry due to Edith's problems with [[tuberculosis]]. When they met again in 1924, Heisman was living in [[Washington, Pennsylvania]], and coaching at Washington and Jefferson College. This time, they did decide to marry, doing it that same year, right before Heisman left Pennsylvania to take his last head coaching job at Rice University in Texas. ==Heisman as an actor== Heisman considered himself an actor as well as coach, and was a part of several acting troupes in the offseason. He was known for delivering grand theatrical speeches to inspire his players, and some considered him to be an eccentric and melodramatic. He was described as exhibiting "the temperament, panache, and audacity of the showman." [[File:John Heisman produced play David Garrick Aubun.png|thumb|Poster for the play ''David Garrick'', produced and acted in by Heisman, Alabama Polytechnic Institute (Auburn) 1897|375x375px]] His 1897 Auburn team finished $700 in debt. To raise money for next season, Heisman created the Alabama Polytechnic Institute (Auburn) Dramatic Club to stage and act as the main character in the comic play ''David Garrick'' by [[Thomas William Robertson]].{{cite web |last=Henderson |first=Jeremy |date=May 30, 2013 |title=Auburn theatrical legend John Heisman put on, starred in play to save Auburn football |url=https://www.thewareaglereader.com/2013/05/auburn-theatrical-legend-john-heisman-put-on-starred-in-play-to-save-auburn-football/ |access-date=September 28, 2025 |website=The War Eagle Reader}} [[George Petrie (American football)|George Petrie]] described the play as "decidedly the most successful event of its kind ever seen in Auburn". A local newspaper, ''The Opelika Post'', reviewed Heisman's performance:
He was naturalness itself, and there was not a single place in which he overdid his part. His changes from drunk to sober and back again in the drunken scene were skillfully done, and the humor of many of his speeches caused a roar of laughter. He acted not like an amateur, but like the skilled professional that he is.
During his time at Auburn, Heisman also took on more serious roles, and was considered as a refined elocutionist when performing Shakespearean plays or reciting his monologues. The next year, the API Dramatic Club performed ''A Scrap of Paper'' by [[Victorien Sardou]]. In May 1898, Heisman appeared in ''[[Diplomacy (play)|Diplomacy]]'', an English adaptation of ''Dora'' by Sardou, with the Mordaunt-Block Stock Company at the [[Herald Square Theatre|Herald Square Theater]] on [[Theater District, Manhattan|Broadway]]. Later that summer, he performed in ''The Ragged Regiment'' by [[Robert Neilson Stephens]] at the Herald Square Theater and ''Caste'' at the Columbus Theater in [[Harlem]].{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=113}} In 1899, he was in the Macdonald Stock Company, which performed at Crump's Park in [[Macon, Georgia]], including the role of Dentatus in ''[[Virginius (play)|Virginius]]'' by [[James Sheridan Knowles]]. When the Macdonald Stock Company took a hiatus in June 1899, Heisman joined the Thanouser-Hatch Company of Atlanta. He performed in at least two plays for this company, in ''Brother John'' by [[Martha Morton]] at the Grand Theater in Atlanta, playing the role of Captain Van Sprague. At the end of Auburn's 1899 season, a public conflict developed between Heisman and umpire W. L. Taylor. Heisman wrote to the ''[[Birmingham Post-Herald|Birmingham Age-Herald]]'' complaining about Taylor's officiating in general and specifically his cancellation of an Auburn touchdown because the scoring play began before the starting whistle following a [[Time-out (sport)|time out]]. In his published reply, Taylor critiqued Heisman as someone with "histrionic gifts," making "lurid appeals," and seeking "peanut gallery applause" for "heroically acted character parts" in some "cheap theater." Heisman responded to that characterization as "The heinous crime I shall neither attempt to palliate nor deny" and that what Taylor said could be a "studied insult to the whole art of acting." In 1900, Heisman joined the Spooner Dramatic Company of [[Tampa, Florida]]. On return from [[Key West]], Heisman got very seasick. By 1901, Heisman joined the Dixie Stock Company, which performed several plays in the Dukate Theater at [[Biloxi, Mississippi]]. There, he received his first major romantic lead, Armand in ''[[La Dame aux Camélias|Camille]]''. In 1902, he managed Crump's Park Stock Company.{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=114}} He started the Heisman Dramatic Stock Company while at Clemson in 1903, which spent much of the summer performing at Riverside Park in [[Asheville, North Carolina]].{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=115}} By 1904, Heisman operated the Heisman Stock Company. It performed at the Casino Theater at Pickett Springs Resort in [[Montgomery, Alabama]]. Their first performance was [[William Gillette]]'s ''Because She Loved Him So''. The next summer opened with a performance at the Grand Opera House in [[Augusta, Georgia]]. In 1906 and 1907, Heisman again performed in Crump's Park in Macon, as well as the Thunderbolt Casino in [[Savannah, Georgia|Savannah]]. In 1906, he purchased an [[Thomas Edison|Edison]] [[Kinetoscope|kinetograph]] for his audiences.{{Harvnb|Heisman|2012|page=116}} By 1908, Heisman managed Heisman Theatrical Enterprises.{{Harvnb|Brandt|2001|page=147}} ==Death and legacy== [[File:John Heisman Statue.jpg|left|thumb|Heisman statue at Georgia Tech.]] Heisman died of pneumonia on October 3, 1936, in New York City. Three days later, his body was taken by train to his wife's hometown of [[Rhinelander, Wisconsin]], where he was buried in Grave{{nbsp}}D, Lot{{nbsp}}11, Block{{nbsp}}3 of the city-owned Forest Home Cemetery.{{cite news|url=http://ad.go.com/ncf/s/1999/1210/225405.html |title=Gravesite Still Draws Visitors |agency=Associated Press |date=December 10, 1999 |access-date=September 23, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071018000442/http://ad.go.com/ncf/s/1999/1210/225405.html |archive-date=October 18, 2007 |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=http://yourhometown.org/page59.html |title=Wisconsin Hometowns |website=yourhometown.org |access-date=September 23, 2007 |archive-date=September 8, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070908153020/http://www.yourhometown.org/page59.html |url-status=dead }} When Heisman died, he was preparing to write a history of football.{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=128}} ===Legacy=== [[File:Matt Leinart's Heisman Trophy.jpg|thumb|180px|A Heisman Trophy]] Heisman was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame as a coach in 1954, a member of the second class of inductees. Heisman was an innovator and "master strategist". He developed one of the first shifts.{{Harvnb|Heisman|1922|page=267}}{{Harvnb|Magee|2012|page=256}} He was a proponent of the legalization of the forward pass. He had both his guards pull to lead an end run and had his center snap the ball. He invented the hidden ball play, and originated the "hike" or "hep" shouted by the quarterback to start each play. He led the effort to cut the game from halves to quarters. He is credited with the idea of listing downs and yardage on the scoreboard, and of putting his quarterback at [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] on defense.{{cite web|url={{College Football HoF/url|id=1297}}|title=John Heisman|publisher=National Football Foundation|access-date=October 8, 2016}}{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=118}} On December 10, 1936, just two months after Heisman's death on October 3, the Downtown Athletic Club trophy was renamed the [[Heisman Trophy|Heisman Memorial Trophy]], and is now given to the player voted as the season's most outstanding collegiate football player.{{Harvnb|Rielly|2009|pages=163–164}} Voters for this award consist primarily of media representatives, who are allocated by regions across the country to filter out possible regional bias, and former recipients. Following the [[bankruptcy]] of the Downtown Athletic Club in 2002, the award is now given out by the Heisman Trust.{{cite web|url=https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/182049/nissan-re-boots-the-heisman-house-in-dallas.html|title=Nissan Re-Boots The Heisman House in Dallas|author=Karl Greenberg|date=September 4, 2012|website=mediadaily.com}} Georgia Tech's basketball team played in Heisman Gym which was named in his honor when it opened in 1938. Located behind the north stands of Grant Field, the gym was the home of Tech basketball until 1956, when the team moved into Alexander Memorial Coliseum. The facility also had a pool, which was used by the Tech swim team, and an Auditorium. After the basketball team left, the gym was used for swimming until 1977, and as an auditorium until the Ferst Center For The Arts opened in 1992. The gym was demolished in 1995.
